paragraphs: Compressing scientific data involves deciding which information can tolerate error. A compressor trained to preserve a physical quantity may protect that quantity while making the reconstructed data less accurate by conventional measures. This paper develops a local geometric explanation of why these objectives can conflict even when the storage budget stays fixed.

The analysis examines how the entropy model, physical observable, and reconstruction metric respond to changes in the compressor’s latent representation. Each favors particular directions in which compression noise should be reduced. Their interaction determines how error is distributed across directions. Within this local theory, when the preferred directions are misaligned, improving preservation of the physical observable at a fixed bitrate necessarily worsens standard reconstruction distortion.

The authors formalize this relationship as a local rate–distortion law and propose a practical diagnostic based on overlap between dominant eigenspaces. Experiments across scientific domains show that this alignment measure correlates with observed tradeoffs. The contribution connects competing compression objectives to measurable representation geometry, helping explain when preserving physics and preserving conventional fidelity pull in different directions.
icml-2026-a-geometric-lens-on-physics-al.tldr: A local geometric theory explains when preserving physical quantities during compression necessarily trades off against reconstruction fidelity.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks repeatedly exchange information between connected nodes. With enough rounds, node representations can become so similar that useful distinctions disappear, a problem called oversmoothing. This paper studies that collapse as a dynamical phenomenon: the network settles into a stable homogeneous fixed point, meaning a state that erases differences and resists small disturbances.

The authors show theoretically that replacing standard monotone activations such as ReLU with a particular class of functions can change this stability. Using Lyapunov–Schmidt reduction, they prove that the substitution induces a bifurcation—a change in the system’s stable states. The homogeneous state becomes unstable, while a pair of stable, non-homogeneous patterns emerges. These patterns provably resist oversmoothing within the analyzed setting.

The theory also predicts a specific scaling law for the strength of the emerging patterns, which experiments quantitatively validate. The authors turn their analysis into a closed-form initialization and demonstrate its usefulness on real benchmarks. The central contribution is a connection between activation choice, stability, and the preservation of distinct node representations in deep graph networks.
icml-2026-beyond-relu-bifurcation-oversm.tldr: A bifurcation analysis shows how changing activation functions can create stable graph representations that resist oversmoothing.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a language model on a narrow task can produce undesirable behavior outside that task, even while the intended skill improves. BLOCK-EM investigates whether this emergent misalignment can be reduced by intervening on the internal features that control it. The approach identifies a small feature set and constrains those features from strengthening during fine-tuning.

Across six fine-tuning domains, constraining a fixed set of features produces up to a 95% relative reduction in emergent misalignment, with no degradation in measured model quality or target-task performance. The authors test the finding using separate feature-selection and evaluation splits, multiple independent judges, and multiple random seeds in key settings. Their ablations support the interpretation that the effect depends on the identified mechanism.

The paper also identifies a limit: prolonged fine-tuning can bring misalignment back. Evidence is consistent with the behavior shifting through other features or layers, and evaluated modifications partially recover the blocking effect. The findings therefore support targeted internal constraints as a training-time mitigation, while showing that the initially identified feature set may not remain sufficient throughout extended training.
icml-2026-block-em-preventing-emergent-m.tldr: Constraining selected internal features substantially reduces emergent misalignment in tested settings, although extended fine-tuning can weaken the protection.

paragraphs: Recognizing familiar concepts in unfamiliar combinations requires more than remembering previously seen inputs. This paper asks what geometry an embedding must have to support that capability. It formalizes three requirements—divisibility, transferability, and stability—and studies the constraints they impose on representations under standard training.

The theoretical result is that satisfying these requirements necessitates a linear decomposition into components for individual concepts, with different concepts represented orthogonally. In geometric terms, concept contributions must combine additively while occupying perpendicular directions. This provides a conditional foundation for the Linear Representation Hypothesis and yields bounds connecting embedding dimension with the number of concepts that can be composed.

Experiments on CLIP, SigLIP, and DINO find partial versions of this structure: concept factors are low-rank and nearly orthogonal. Stronger evidence of this geometry correlates with better generalization to unseen combinations. The empirical result supports the theoretical picture without establishing that these models fully satisfy its requirements. Together, the findings identify representation structure associated with compositional capability and describe geometry that larger models may approach as they scale.
icml-2026-compositional-generalization-r.tldr: Under three formal requirements and standard training, compositional generalization requires linear concept components that are orthogonal across concepts.

paragraphs: Many convex optimization problems combine a smooth objective with a nonsmooth regularizer. This paper analyzes two classical stochastic methods for that setting, focusing on the quality of the final iterate produced after training. This matters because a guarantee about the last iterate directly describes the point where the algorithm stops.

The first method uses proximal stochastic gradient updates with a single regularizer. The second handles a regularizer made from many nonsmooth functions by randomly selecting one function’s proximal operator at each step. The analysis relaxes the bounded-variance assumption commonly used to establish last-iterate guarantees. Under componentwise convexity and smoothness, both methods achieve a convergence rate proportional to one over the square root of the iteration count, up to logarithmic factors.

That rate is optimal apart from those logarithmic terms. The results also apply directly to graph-guided regularization in multi-task and federated learning, where regularization contributions correspond to edges in a collaboration graph. The contribution strengthens the theoretical justification for familiar algorithms in structured problems while reducing reliance on a stringent noise assumption.
icml-2026-convergence-rate-of-the-last-i.tldr: Two stochastic proximal methods obtain nearly optimal last-iterate convergence guarantees while relaxing the usual bounded-variance assumption.

paragraphs: Dictionary learning tries to express complex embeddings through a collection of features that can help reveal a model’s internal structure. Sparse autoencoders are a popular approach, but they use a simple linear encoder for a sparse encoding subproblem that is NP-hard. This paper asks whether a more elaborate optimization method can provide a useful alternative at transformer scale.

The proposed Double-Batch KSVD adapts the classical KSVD algorithm to datasets with millions of samples and thousands of dimensions. It brings a different optimization approach to the same broad disentangling problem, creating a way to assess whether sparse autoencoders’ simpler encoding procedure still finds strong solutions in practice.

The authors evaluate text embeddings from Gemma-2-2B and Pythia-160M using six SAEBench metrics and obtain results competitive with established sparse autoencoder approaches. Image embeddings from DINOv2-S and DINOv2-B show similar results. Matching performance through a different method suggests that sparse autoencoders already find strong dictionary-learning solutions, while demonstrating that traditional optimization can scale to these problem sizes. The findings support both approaches as useful directions for interpretability research.
icml-2026-db-ksvd-scalable-alternating-o.tldr: DB-KSVD scales classical dictionary learning to transformer embeddings and achieves results competitive with sparse autoencoders.

paragraphs: Differentially private language-model training must control the influence of individual training examples. Computing the gradient norms needed for clipping can become expensive as context length and model width increase. The paper identifies a memory bottleneck in existing fast clipping implementations whose overhead grows with batch size and the smaller of squared sequence length and squared layer width.

DP-SGD-RC replaces the relevant norm-estimation computation with randomized clipping based on stochastic trace estimation. It uses Hutchinson’s estimator and Hutch++, which reduce the memory footprint of estimating per-sample gradient norms. Because randomness enters the clipping procedure itself, the authors provide a privacy analysis for the resulting algorithm and show noise multipliers competitive with deterministic clipping.

Experiments fine-tune Llama 3.2 1B on long-context classification, question answering, and summarization benchmarks. In these evaluations, the method matches baseline utility while substantially reducing memory and computation. The contribution connects a cheaper estimation procedure with a formal privacy analysis, showing how the cost of privacy-preserving fine-tuning can be reduced without losing the measured task quality in the reported settings.
icml-2026-efficient-dp-sgd-for-llms-with.tldr: Randomized gradient clipping reduces private LLM fine-tuning costs while preserving competitive privacy noise levels and measured task utility.

paragraphs: Even ordinary gradient descent can have complicated behavior when used to train nonlinear models. Its trajectories, oscillating objective values, and sometimes unexpectedly fast progress remain difficult to explain. This paper develops a different mathematical description of those dynamics by connecting gradient descent with generalized perceptron algorithms.

For the nonlinear models studied with logistic loss, the authors show that gradient descent steps reduce to simpler perceptron-style updates. This representation makes classical linear algebra tools available for analyzing the training process. The point is to expose structure in familiar gradient descent dynamics through an equivalent, more tractable description.

On a minimal example, the analysis proves that nonlinearity in a two-layer model can reduce iteration complexity to roughly the square root of the feature count, ignoring logarithmic factors, compared with a linear lower bound for linear models. Extensive numerical experiments support the theoretical results. The demonstrated acceleration belongs to the analyzed example, but it provides a concrete explanation of how model nonlinearity itself can contribute to faster optimization without introducing an explicit acceleration mechanism.
icml-2026-gradient-descent-as-a-perceptr.tldr: A perceptron-based view of gradient descent explains how nonlinearity can provably accelerate optimization in a minimal two-layer example.

paragraphs: Adversarial prompts face competing requirements: they must induce a targeted response, remain linguistically coherent, and preserve the attacker’s intended meaning. The paper argues that existing optimization approaches often generate conspicuous suffixes, while attempts to improve coherence can reduce success or change the query enough that the response no longer serves the original goal.

Greedy Coordinate Diffusion uses the generative priors of discrete diffusion language models to guide the search for adversarial suffixes. Its purpose is to combine coherence with semantic adherence, so success reflects the intended request rather than a substantially altered one. Unlike Greedy Coordinate Gradient, the framework does not need direct gradient access and operates in a gray-box setting.

In the reported comparisons, GCD achieves the highest attack success rate while remaining competitive on response-quality scores. Its prompts are also detected less frequently by perplexity-based and guard-model filters than those produced by other methods. These findings show that linguistic naturalness and resistance to the tested filters can coexist with effective attacks, making coherence an important dimension when evaluating model defenses.
icml-2026-greedy-coordinate-diffusion-ef.tldr: Diffusion-guided adversarial prompts combine strong reported attack success with coherent language and lower detection rates under the tested filters.

paragraphs: Predicting among millions of possible labels makes a classifier’s output layer expensive to store and compute. Simply removing connections may reduce arithmetic without providing comparable speedups, because irregular access patterns waste hardware capacity. HASTE addresses this gap by designing output-layer sparsity around both label relationships and efficient GPU execution.

Semantically related labels share a sparse pattern of input features while keeping separate weights. This reduces index storage and reuses features across labels, while encouraging related outputs to draw on similar information. Custom CUDA kernels exploit the structure. The method also separates frequent labels into a small dense head and places the remaining labels in a sparse tail, maintaining an informative gradient pathway.

Kernel benchmarks report up to 4.4 times faster forward passes and up to 25 times faster backward passes than standard fixed fan-in sparsity, with performance within a few percent of a dense bottleneck matched for arithmetic count. On large-scale extreme multi-label benchmarks, HASTE matches or improves precision@k over prior sparse baselines and narrows the gap to dense models. The results link a particular sparsity structure to practical computational gains.
icml-2026-haste-hardware-aware-dynamic-s.tldr: HASTE groups related labels around shared sparse feature patterns to turn output-layer sparsity into practical GPU speedups.

paragraphs: Recognizing colors and shapes is different from identifying which color belongs to which shape. This binding problem is difficult for vision–language embedding models such as CLIP. The paper investigates an apparent contradiction: cross-modal retrieval behaves as though concepts are unstructured, yet object information can be recovered from image embeddings and text embeddings separately.

The authors analyze the binding function that maps concepts into a scene embedding. They find that scene embeddings split additively into object representations, explaining why probes operating within one modality can recover objects. However, CLIP’s binding function has high complexity. The authors suggest that this likely obstructs learning a shared image–text binding mechanism that transfers to unseen concept combinations.

Controlled transformer models trained from scratch show that the limitation is not fundamental to embedding models. With sufficient data coverage, binding generalization emerges, accompanied by simpler binding functions involving multiplicative interactions between concepts. The findings distinguish having object information inside each representation from organizing that information in a shared, generalizable way across modalities. They also identify a setting in which systematic binding can be learned.
icml-2026-how-can-embedding-models-bind-.tldr: CLIP contains recoverable object information, while controlled models show that simpler binding functions can support generalization with sufficient data coverage.

paragraphs: Long-term fairness concerns how decisions and population behavior influence each other over time. A central difficulty is that outcomes may only become visible after a positive decision: repayment is observed when a loan is granted. This paper studies fairness under these selective labels and analytically shows that naive approaches do not guarantee fairness.

The framework combines observed outcomes with a model that predicts missing labels. It expresses the true fairness measure in terms of observed fairness and bias from those predictions. Using confidence in the predictor, the authors derive sufficient conditions for satisfying true fairness from quantities that can actually be observed. These conditions connect uncertainty about unobserved outcomes with the fairness assessment.

The theory then informs a reinforcement learning algorithm for sequential decision-making. In semisynthetic environments, the algorithm achieves fairness and performance comparable to an agent given the true labels. The result supports accounting explicitly for selective observation when optimizing long-term policy behavior. Its guarantee depends on the stated sufficient conditions, while the empirical comparison shows how the approach performs in the evaluated environments.
icml-2026-long-term-fairness-with-select.tldr: A predictor-aware fairness framework supports long-term decision-making when outcomes are only observed after positive decisions.

paragraphs: Accelerated gradient methods have optimal convergence guarantees for convex functions with uniformly bounded curvature. This paper studies a more flexible smoothness condition in which the curvature bound depends on gradient magnitude through a function called ell. The condition includes both standard smoothness and the generalized setting parameterized by L0 and L1.

Previous accelerated guarantees in this broader setting could introduce dependence on the starting gradient, exponential factors, or expensive auxiliary procedures. The authors develop new proof techniques that achieve oracle complexity proportional to the square root of ell at zero, multiplied by the starting distance to an optimum and divided by the square root of the target error. This holds for sufficiently small error tolerance and virtually any ell.

For the L0–L1 case, the resulting small-error bound depends on the square root of L0 and is provably optimal in that regime. It removes the nonconstant multiplicative factors present in prior accelerated algorithms. The contribution resolves whether classical acceleration-like accuracy dependence remains achievable under this broader curvature model, while retaining the explicit qualification that the stated rate concerns small error tolerances.
icml-2026-near-optimal-convergence-of-ac.tldr: New analysis establishes near-optimal accelerated convergence under generalized smoothness in the small-error regime.

paragraphs: Prover–verifier games offer a route toward verifiable nonlinear classification, but applying them to complex images has been difficult. Concept encodings can translate such inputs into interpretable information, although they are often paired with relatively limited linear predictors. Neural Concept Verifier combines these approaches to support more expressive decisions over structured concepts.

The framework first uses minimally supervised concept discovery models to extract encodings from raw inputs. A prover selects a subset of those encodings, and a nonlinear verifier bases its decision exclusively on that subset. This makes the selected concept information the verifier’s entire input, connecting the decision process to the evidence supplied through the prover–verifier structure.

On high-dimensional datasets with logically complex classification problems, NCV outperforms classic concept-based models and pixel-based prover–verifier classifiers. The evaluations also show that it helps mitigate shortcut behavior. The contribution is a unified framework that brings concept discovery into a formal-verifiability approach, with empirical results supporting its usefulness for more complex inputs. The authors present it as a step toward concept-level verifiable AI.
icml-2026-neural-concept-verifier-scalin.tldr: Neural Concept Verifier combines discovered concepts with prover–verifier games to improve classification and reduce shortcut behavior on complex inputs.

paragraphs: Group counterfactual explanations describe how instances in a group could change to receive different model outcomes. Existing approaches can require fresh optimization for new members, depend strongly on classifier assumptions, or distort relationships within the group. This paper learns an explicit mapping from original instances to their counterfactual counterparts.

The mapping is formulated through optimal transport, minimizing the group’s total movement cost. Once learned, it can produce a counterfactual for a new group instance without solving the optimization again. Using fewer parameters also makes the shared actionable change easier to interpret. For linear classifiers, the authors derive the functions through mathematical optimization and identify the relevant convex problem types, including quadratic and quadratically constrained quadratic programs.

Experiments show accurate generalization to new instances, preservation of group geometry, and only negligible additional transport cost compared with baseline methods. When classifier linearity cannot be exploited, the approach also substantially outperforms the baselines. The contribution combines reusable counterfactual generation with explicit attention to the structure of the whole group, rather than treating each explanation as an unrelated individual adjustment.
icml-2026-optimal-transport-group-counte.tldr: Learned optimal transport maps generate reusable group counterfactuals while preserving group geometry and keeping movement costs competitive.

paragraphs: Foundation models can make confident predictions even when their uncertainty is poorly calibrated. Ensembles help quantify uncertainty by combining multiple models, but independently training and storing large members is expensive. Singular Value Ensemble offers a parameter-efficient alternative by sharing most of the representation structure across members.

Its central assumption is that the singular vectors of weight matrices identify meaningful, orthogonal knowledge directions. SVE freezes these directions and trains a separate set of singular values for each member, changing how strongly each shared direction contributes. Random initialization and random batch sampling during joint training produce different combinations of the same underlying basis, supplying ensemble diversity without separate full models.

Across evaluated language and vision tasks with different backbones, SVE performs comparably to an explicit ensemble while adding less than 1% to the base model’s parameter count. It improves calibration while maintaining predictive accuracy. These findings support rescaling shared representation directions as an economical source of useful model diversity. The interpretation rests on the stated knowledge-direction assumption, and the reported parameter savings describe the additional learned parameters.
icml-2026-quantifying-the-uncertainty-of.tldr: Singular Value Ensemble improves uncertainty calibration by varying shared representation strengths with less than 1% additional parameters.

paragraphs: Text-to-image models can encode attributes that appear only rarely in their outputs. Audits built around predefined fairness categories may miss these features, while analyses of dominant attributes emphasize what the model produces most often. RAIGen targets the complementary problem of discovering underrepresented social, cultural, or stylistic attributes without predefined minority labels.

The framework uses Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders to identify interpretable neurons in model representations. A minority metric combines how frequently a neuron activates with how semantically distinctive it is. Images that activate selected neurons most strongly then reveal the associated rare attributes. Combining frequency and distinctiveness connects rarity to interpretable content rather than treating infrequent activation alone as the discovery.

Experiments show that RAIGen finds attributes beyond fixed fairness categories in Stable Diffusion and scales to larger models such as SDXL. It supports systematic auditing across architectures and targeted amplification of rare attributes during generation. The contribution is a discovery framework for underrepresented features already encoded in the model, allowing auditing and generation control to extend beyond categories chosen in advance.
icml-2026-raigen-rare-attribute-identifi.tldr: RAIGen discovers and helps amplify rare attributes encoded in diffusion models without requiring predefined minority categories.

paragraphs: Discovering causal relationships in time series is difficult because noise can make unrelated variation look like meaningful influence. This paper addresses that problem through the frequency structure of the data. The authors observe that many real-world time series have power-law spectra, a pattern they connect notably to self-organizing behavior.

Their method extracts spectral features based on this power-law structure to amplify genuine causal signals. The key choice is to use the way variation is distributed across frequencies as information for causal discovery. This brings a recurring property of real-world stochastic signals into the design of the inference method, with robustness to noise as the motivating objective.

The authors report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art alternatives on synthetic benchmarks and real-world datasets with known causal structures. Those known structures allow inferred relationships to be checked against a reference, giving the comparisons a direct basis for assessing causal recovery. The findings support the practical value of power-law spectral features in the evaluated settings, connecting a statistical regularity in time series with more reliable causal inference.
icml-2026-robust-causal-discovery-in-rea.tldr: Power-law spectral features improve reported causal discovery performance on noisy synthetic and real-world time series.

paragraphs: Causal discovery methods often simplify their task by excluding feedback loops, assuming Gaussian noise, or requiring knowledge of which variables an experiment changed. SCOUT addresses a setting where nonlinear relationships may form cycles and the targets of soft interventions are unknown. This brings several difficulties together within one causal-learning problem.

The framework maximizes the likelihood of observed data to recover the graph structure. It uses two normalizing-flow architectures: contractive residual flows and neural spline flows. These provide the modeling machinery for learning nonlinear cyclic relationships from interventional observations, while the method also seeks to recover the unknown intervention targets.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show that SCOUT outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both graph recovery and target recovery across varied intervention and noise settings. The findings support tackling feedback, nonlinearity, and unidentified interventions jointly rather than requiring those aspects to be simplified away beforehand. The contribution is a framework and empirical evidence for causal discovery under this more flexible combination of conditions, with evaluation covering both the causal structure and the interventions that help reveal it.
icml-2026-scout-cyclic-causal-discovery-.tldr: SCOUT learns nonlinear causal graphs with feedback loops and unknown soft-intervention targets using normalizing flows.

paragraphs: Learning tasks sequentially can cause a neural network to lose skills acquired earlier, a problem called catastrophic forgetting. Shapley Neuron Valuation addresses this by deciding which neurons should be protected when training moves to a new task. Its aim is to balance preserving existing knowledge with retaining enough flexibility to learn.

The framework grounds neuron importance in cooperative game theory through Shapley valuation. It selectively freezes neurons judged important while allowing the remaining neurons to change. This makes the importance estimate operational: it determines where adaptation is permitted. The resulting continual-learning method uses no replay buffer and does not expand the network architecture.

On ImageNet-1k, SNV consistently outperforms the evaluated buffer-free methods. The abstract reports accuracy improvements of +2.88% in class-incremental learning and +6.46% in task-incremental learning relative to the second baseline. These results support selective preservation of neurons as a way to reduce forgetting within a fixed network. The contribution combines a principled importance framework with a direct training rule and evidence across two continual-learning scenarios.
icml-2026-shapley-neuron-values-for-cont.tldr: Shapley-based neuron importance guides selective freezing to improve continual learning without replay buffers or network expansion.

paragraphs: State-space language models such as Mamba make inference efficient, but their large parameter counts still complicate deployment. Generic pruning methods overlook an important architectural detail: the state-transition matrix is discretized and shared across time. SparseSSM adapts pruning to that structure so that weight importance reflects how the state-space module actually operates.

The framework extends optimal brain surgeon pruning through a layer-wise, approximate second-order importance score. It aggregates Hessian-trace information across time steps, incorporating curvature information from the repeated use of parameters. A separate component-sensitivity analysis guides pruning of feed-forward networks and helps identify where redundancy lies within Mamba.

The authors report removing 50% of SSM weights without fine-tuning while observing limited performance degradation, and describe the method as state of the art for one-shot pruning of Mamba-based language models. The framework can also extend to semi-structured and structured sparsity and other state-space architectures. Its main contribution is architecture-aware, training-free compression: repeated temporal use of state-space parameters becomes part of the pruning decision rather than being ignored.
icml-2026-sparsessm-efficient-selective-.tldr: SparseSSM accounts for state-space dynamics to prune 50% of SSM weights without fine-tuning and with limited reported degradation.

paragraphs: Large reasoning models can struggle with spatial tasks despite their broad capabilities. This paper argues that, for many tasks, relevant spatial abilities already exist in pretrained models but need better internal alignment. It investigates whether logical consistency can provide a training signal without ground-truth spatial annotations.

The proposed self-supervised reinforcement learning framework targets the chain-of-thought process. Consistency verifiers check geometric and semantic relationships under transformations such as flipping a scene or swapping the order of objects in a question. The authors optimize these rewards with OT-GRPO, a minimal-consistency matching variant of group relative policy optimization. The training signal comes from relationships that the model’s reasoning should preserve across transformed questions.

The reported results show that models can improve their spatial logic through this label-free training. Accuracy approaches that of models trained with ground-truth supervision, with similar generalization across diverse tasks and domains. These findings support internal consistency as a useful source of supervision for spatial reasoning. They also give empirical backing to the claim that some observed failures reflect how existing capabilities are expressed, rather than solely a lack of spatial knowledge.
icml-2026-the-art-of-interrogation-consi.tldr: Training reasoning models for geometric and semantic consistency improves spatial reasoning without ground-truth labels.

paragraphs: A stronger student model can learn from a weaker teacher, but unreliable teacher labels can interfere with that learning. This paper treats weak-to-strong generalization primarily as a data-selection problem. It introduces trust functions that assign a scalar reliability score to each weak label and use those scores to filter the training supervision.

Across domains including world knowledge, quantitative reasoning, and decision-making, students trained with trust filtering match and sometimes exceed the performance obtained with ground-truth supervision. The method also supports an iterative chain: a trained student becomes the next teacher, allowing gains to accumulate. In the reported study, this chain produces the strongest final model.

The authors’ analyses suggest that filtering helps through more than simply removing incorrect labels. Neural trust functions create an implicit easy-first curriculum, recover near-optimal alternatives when ground-truth labels are incomplete, and yield more coherent gradient updates. These proposed mechanisms help explain the observed stability and efficiency. The contribution links supervision quality to selective trust, with empirical evidence that carefully chosen weak labels can support strong learning across several domains.
icml-2026-trust-functions-near-lossless-.tldr: Trust-based filtering lets stronger students learn from weaker teachers and match or sometimes exceed ground-truth supervision in reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Continuous normalizing flows generate samples through an evolving trajectory, making sampling iterative and intermediate states difficult to interpret. This paper seeks to accelerate generation while preserving the teacher model’s dynamics along the whole path. Its approach uses Koopman theory to represent nonlinear flow evolution through a linear operator in a higher-dimensional space.

The method lifts Conditional Flow Matching into this space and trains for infinitesimal consistency with the teacher’s vector field throughout generation. A practical, simulation-free objective enforces this alignment. Preserving intermediate dynamics is central: the learned operator is intended to describe how generation unfolds, giving it a role beyond reproducing the final output.

The resulting sampling procedure is one-step and parallelizable. The operator also enables analysis and control through semantically coherent editing directions, inversion aligned with the teacher, and class-conditional spectral signatures. Experiments show competitive sample quality alongside these capabilities. The contribution connects faster sampling with a representation of the full generative process, making the linearized dynamics useful for both producing samples and examining the trajectories that lead to them.
icml-2026-unfolding-generative-flows-wit.tldr: Koopman-based linearization enables one-step flow sampling while preserving teacher dynamics for trajectory analysis and control.

paragraphs: Coding agents can improve other agents by editing and evaluating the code that governs their execution. Studying this capability is difficult because an agent harness mixes deterministic software with stochastic language-model outputs. Understanding an edit’s effect therefore requires tracking both intermediate behavior and downstream task results.

VeRO provides an outer harness for this optimization process. It maintains versioned snapshots of target harnesses, controls evaluation budgets, and captures structured execution traces. These features organize the evidence needed to compare successive changes. The accompanying VeRO-Bench supplies target agents, tasks, and reference evaluation procedures, creating a common setting for studying how optimizers modify agent systems.

Using this infrastructure, the authors conduct an empirical comparison of optimizers across tasks and analyze which modifications reliably improve target harnesses. The contribution combines research tooling with a benchmark and a study of agent optimization behavior. By making versions, evaluation resources, and execution observations explicit, VeRO supports systematic investigation of coding agents’ ability to improve other agents through iterative code changes.
icml-2026-vero-a-harness-for-agents-to-o.tldr: VeRO provides versioning, controlled evaluation, execution traces, and a benchmark for studying how coding agents improve other agents.
